newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy grew at nine-year high in first quarter.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy grew at nine-year high in first quarter.

text.p: U.S. economic growth swept ahead at its fastest pace in more than nine years during the first quarter this year, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday, but price rises also accelerated sharply.

Gross domestic product expanded at a surprising 5.6 percent annual rate in the first three months of this year. That was a strong pickup from a 3.8 percent rate of growth in last year's final quarter as a wave of consumer spending, business investment and inventory-building pushed national economic activity to a heightened pace.

The first-quarter GDP performance was much stronger than Wall Street economists' forecasts for a 4.1 percent rate of growth. Commerce said the first-quarter GDP rise would have been even greater except for a pickup in imports and a slowing in exports of American-made products to foreign markets.
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced within U.S. borders.
Prices also moved ahead strongly, however, in a potentially troubling sign for inflation. The rate of increase in prices reflected in the first-quarter GDP report was the strongest in two years.
The initial estimate of first-quarter GDP will be revised twice in coming months to arrive at a final official figure.

"The acceleration in first-quarter growth was more than accounted for by a turnaround in inventory investment, an acceleration in consumer spending and a turnaround in business investment in producers' durable equipment," the Commerce Department said.

Personal consumption spending -- the most potent force in the U.S. economy -- surged at a 6.4 percent or $73.5-billion-a-year pace in the first quarter, nearly twice the 3.4 percent or $39-billion rise posted in last year's final quarter.
The department said it was the most vigorous pickup in consumer spending in nine years, since a 7.2 percent jump in the first quarter of 1988.

Commerce said that businesses increased their inventories of goods ready for sale early this year at nearly three times the rate they did in last year's fourth quarter, evidently anticipating that brisk consumer spending will continue.

Inventories grew at a $46.1-billion rate in the first quarter, compared with $17.1 billion in last year's final quarter. Production for inventories boosts overall GDP in the period in which it happens.

Corporate investment to expand operations also was strong in the first quarter as businesses planned for rising levels of activity. Spending on producers' durable equipment shot up at an $18.2-billion annual rate or 12.9 percent after contracting by $1.3 billion or 0.9 percent in the fourth quarter last year.

Two inflation measures in the GDP report pointed to a a speedup in the rate of price rises. The implicit price deflator advanced at a 2.3 percent annual rate after a 1.5 percent rise in the fourth quarter last year -- the sharpest advance since a 2.4 percent rise in the second quarter of 1995.

The report's fixed-weight measure of price changes advanced at a 2.7 percent pace after a 1.7 percent gain in the fourth quarter last year. The department said that was the strongest rise in the price measure since a 3.3 percent increase in the first quarter of 1995.
